meta.title: Who really said "In theory there is no difference between theory and practice; in practice there is"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Yogi Berra. The line appeared in a Yale Literary Magazine essay by Benjamin Brewster in February 1882, decades before Berra was born.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In theory there is no difference between theory and practice; in practice there is'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Yogi Berra. Quote Investigator traces it to Benjamin Brewster in The Yale Literary Magazine, February 1882.

answer.label: Not Yogi Berra — actually Benjamin Brewster
answer.authorDates: Yale College class of 1882 · student essayist
answer.sourceLine: The line was already in print in The Yale Literary Magazine for February 1882, in an undergraduate essay titled “Theory and Practice” signed Benjamin Brewster — decades before Yogi Berra was born. Quote Investigator ↗ credits Brewster with originating the saying; there is no evidence Berra ever said it.
answer.confidenceText: The wording is documented in an 1882 magazine essay; the attribution to Yogi Berra is unsupported.

source.heading: Where the line actually appears

docMeta.dd: The Yale Literary Magazine, vol. 47, no. 5, p. 202

source.excerpt: I heard no more, for I was lost in self-reproach that I had been the victim of ‘vulgar error.’ But afterwards, a kind of haunting doubt came over me. What does his lucid explanation amount to but this, that in theory there is no difference between theory and practice, while in practice there is?
trail: February 1882 — earliest strong match located by Quote Investigator ↗: Benjamin Brewster’s essay “Theory and Practice” in The Yale Literary Magazine, p. 202.
1961 — Charles F. Kettering publishes a related remark; QI ↗ calls it a variant, published 1961, not the 1882 saying itself.

1984 — Walter J. Savitch’s programming textbook prints “In theory, there is no difference between theory and practice; but in practice, there is” and credits it only as a remark overheard at a computer science conference — still anonymous, per Quote Investigator ↗.
Later — named attributions attach themselves, Yogi Berra among them; Wikiquote ↗ notes the saying circulated anonymously for more than a decade before those names appeared.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from the February 1882 issue. Note the original phrasing — “while in practice there is” — and that Brewster frames it as a wry summary of someone else’s argument, not a maxim.

source.rightsNote: The Yale Literary Magazine, vol. 47, no. 5, was published in February 1882 — far earlier than 1931, so the issue and Brewster’s essay are in the public domain in the United States. The Online Books Page ↗ lists digitized runs of the magazine as freely available.

author.name: Benjamin Brewster
author.heading: Who was Benjamin Brewster?
author.metaLine: Yale College class of 1882 · essayist, The Yale Literary Magazine
author.bio: Almost nothing is known about him beyond the byline. Quote Investigator identifies the author of the February 1882 essay “Theory and Practice” as a Benjamin Brewster of the Yale class of 1882 — a student writing for his college literary magazine. Wikiquote files the quotation under the Standard Oil financier of the same name while cautioning that the student essayist was almost certainly a different Benjamin Brewster, so the line should not be pinned to the industrialist.

misattribution.heading: The names it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: This is a genuinely old, genuinely anonymous joke that has been handed to four different famous men, none of whom have any documented claim to it.

items.why: Berra was born in 1925 — long after the saying was in print. Wikiquote ↗ lists it in his Misattributed section, noting it circulated anonymously before names began to appear.
Quote Investigator ↗ points out the expression was already in print before Einstein had reached his third birthday.
Like Berra, Feynman was not yet born when the saying appeared in 1882, and QI ↗ finds no substantive reason to credit him.

items.who: Jan L. A. van de Snepscheut
items.scope: the modern “but in practice, there is” wording
items.why: The Dutch computer scientist is the name most often attached in tech circles, but his own Wikiquote page ↗ places the line under Misattributed and traces it back to the 1882 Yale text.

Kettering did craft a remark published in 1961, but it runs differently — ending on the point that practice will not let you forget or leave anything out. QI ↗ calls it a variant, published 1961, not the 1882 saying itself.

misattribution.truthLine: The credit belongs to Benjamin Brewster, whose essay “Theory and Practice” carried the line in The Yale Literary Magazine for February 1882, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Yogi
lead: Yogi Berra was a genuinely funny man who really did say a lot of paradoxical things, and that reputation works like flypaper. Once a line has the right shape — a sentence that folds back on itself and lands on a shrug — the culture files it under Yogi and stops asking questions.

The theory/practice joke has the shape but not the pedigree. It circulated for a century largely unsigned: Quote Investigator ↗ notes that Walter J. Savitch’s 1984 programming textbook printed it as a “remark overheard at a computer science conference,” with no name attached at all. The famous names were bolted on later.
context.detailsSummary: The near-misses and the variant that is real
detailsBody: Charles F. Kettering, the General Motors engineer, did craft a related remark that saw print in 1961 — but his version runs differently, ending on the idea that practice will not let you forget or leave anything out. It is a cousin of the 1882 line, not the same line.

Computer scientist Jan L. A. van de Snepscheut is the other name most often attached. His Wikiquote page ↗ puts the quotation squarely in its Misattributed section and points back to the same 1882 Yale text.
context.pull: An anonymous joke with a good punchline will eventually find a famous mouth to live in.
